```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 3.5)
```

flexCountReg fits the same regression model with many count distributions.
This vignette shows a workflow for choosing among them: fit candidate
families, compare their fit statistics, and check how well each one
reproduces the observed counts.

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
data("washington_roads")
```

The `washington_roads` data contain crashes on 507 road segments observed
over three years. We model total crashes as a function of traffic volume
(`lnaadt`) and the speed-limit indicator `speed50`, with segment length as
an exposure offset.

## Fitting candidate families

`countreg()` takes the distribution as `family`. Gradient-based optimizers
(`method = "BFGS"` or `"NR"`) are usually the fastest choice for the
closed-form families.

```{r fits}
f <- Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + speed50
fit <- function(family) {
  countreg(f, data = washington_roads, family = family, offset = "lnlength",
           method = "BFGS")
}
models <- list(
  Poisson = fit("Poisson"),
  NB1 = fit("NB1"),
  NB2 = fit("NB2"),
  PIG1 = fit("PIG1"),
  GP1 = fit("GP1")
)
```

## Comparing fit statistics

`glance()` gives one row of fit statistics per model, so the candidates can
be compared side by side.

```{r glance}
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(nm) {
  cbind(model = nm, glance(models[[nm]])[, c("logLik", "AIC", "BIC", "df")])
}))
```

The Poisson model fits far worse than the overdispersed families. For a
single model, `summary()` reports a likelihood-ratio test against the
Poisson model with the same mean specification:

```{r summary}
summary(models$NB2)
```

`regCompTest()` compares two fitted models directly, treating the one with
fewer parameters as the restricted model:

```{r lrtest}
regCompTest(models$Poisson, model2 = models$NB2)$statistics
```

and `regCompTable()` builds a coefficient table across models:

```{r table}
regCompTable(models[c("Poisson", "NB1", "NB2")])
```

McFadden's pseudo R-squared compares each model with the same baseline, an
intercept-only Poisson model (the base count model), so the values are
comparable across distributions. A different baseline can be chosen with the
`basemodel` and `variables` arguments of `regCompTable()` and
`regCompTest()`.

## Does the model reproduce the counts?

Information criteria rank models, but they do not show *where* a model
fails. A rootogram compares the observed frequency of each count with the
frequency expected under the fitted model, on a square-root scale. Bars
hang from the expected curve; a bar that ends above zero means the count is
over-predicted, one that ends below zero means it is under-predicted.

```{r rootograms}
oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
rootogram(models$Poisson, main = "Poisson")
rootogram(models$NB2, main = "NB2")
par(oldpar)
```

The Poisson model under-predicts zeros and large counts, the typical
signature of overdispersion. NB2 tracks the observed frequencies closely.

Randomized quantile residuals are standard normal when the model is
correct, for any count distribution, so a normal Q-Q plot is a useful check:

```{r qq}
set.seed(1)
oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
for (nm in c("Poisson", "NB2")) {
  r <- residuals(models[[nm]], type = "quantile")
  qqnorm(r, main = nm, pch = 20, col = "grey40")
  abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick")
}
par(oldpar)
```

A CURE plot (cumulative residuals against fitted values or a covariate) is
another standard diagnostic in safety analysis:

```{r cure, eval = FALSE}
cureplot(models$NB2, indvar = "lnaadt", n_resamples = 20)
```

## Modeling the dispersion and the zeros

The distribution parameters can depend on covariates. Here the NB2
dispersion depends on the speed-limit indicator:

```{r generalized}
nb2_gen <- countreg(f, data = washington_roads, family = "NB2",
                    offset = "lnlength",
                    dis_param_formula_1 = ~ speed50, method = "BFGS")
tidy(nb2_gen, conf.int = TRUE)
```

When there are more zeros than a count distribution allows, a zero-inflated
or hurdle version of any family can be fitted with `zero_formula`:

```{r zinb}
zinb <- countreg(f, data = washington_roads, family = "NB2",
                 offset = "lnlength", zero_formula = ~ 1, method = "NR")
c(NB2 = as.numeric(logLik(models$NB2)), ZINB = as.numeric(logLik(zinb)))
# Estimated probability of a structural zero
unname(plogis(coef(zinb)["Zero:(Intercept)"]))
```

Here the probability of a structural zero is estimated at essentially zero
and the log-likelihood equals that of NB2: the zeros are already explained
by the negative binomial, so the zero-inflated model adds nothing. (When an
estimate is at the boundary like this, its standard error is not
meaningful.)

## Using the chosen model

Predictions have one value per row of new data. Besides the expected count,
`predict()` gives the probability of each count:

```{r predict}
nd <- washington_roads[1:3, ]
predict(models$NB2, newdata = nd)
round(predict(models$NB2, newdata = nd, type = "prob", max_count = 4), 3)
```

Marginal effects (or elasticities) on the expected count come from
`margEffTable()`:

```{r margeff}
margEffTable(models$NB2)
```
